utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Turone and I appear today with Mr. Cowles and Mr. Huber for the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have appearances for the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Eugene O'Sullivan, I appear on behalf of Mr. Delalic and my colleague and lead counsel, Ms. Residovic, will not be here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: My name is Niko Djuric, attorney at law from Zagreb, Croatia, and today I appear on behalf of the defendant, Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic and I am defending Mr. Hazim Delic, together with me defending him is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Cynthia McMurrey. I represent Esad Landzo, along with Ms. Nancy Boler and Mr. Calvin Saunders. Thank You.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, in order to avoid any problems with this mistaken identity of appearances here. In the transcript, I seem to be confused with Mr. Olujic and I would like the record to reflect that this is not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is no way of mistaking the two of you. Kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Damir Gogic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McMurrey, can we hear you and your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may if you are Mrs. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just so we don't get confused with those twins again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I consider that as a compliment, but -- Examined by Ms. Boler:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gogic, please state your name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Couldn't hear the witness. There is no interpretation. I cannot hear the interpretation into Bosnian. Yes, I can hear it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Gogic Damir. I come from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, sit down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that I am Nancy Boler and along with Cynthia McMurrey and Calvin Saunders, I represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, I haven't heard the interpretation well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, he just stated that he did not hear the interpretation well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you to explain to the Court what your current occupation is and where you are stationed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an officer in the Army of the Federation. I reside in Konjic and I work in Bugojno. It's about 110 kilometres from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you and I have met before. We met last night when I came to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just briefly a couple of weeks ago with my last visit to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we spoke again last night at your hotel when you arrived in The Hague, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you just a little bit about the events of yesterday when you were travelling to The Hague. Is it true that you travelled from Konjic to the Sarajevo airport with another witness, potential defence witness, whose name was Mehmedalija Rizvic, nickname Hodza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mehmedalija Rizvic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court to the best of your knowledge why Mr. Rizvic is not here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the way from Konjic to Sarajevo, in the car, he felt sick. And at the airport he went into the bathroom, he was vomiting and he wasn't able to get on the plane and come here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also expecting another defence witness named Senad Nemic to join you at the airport; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he never showed up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't show up. Attorney from Konjic, Asim Suta, told me he will be waiting at the airport. However, he wasn't there and I have no idea what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the years before the war. You and Esad Landzo grew up together in Konjic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your family and Esad Landzo's family lived on the same street, the 15th of September Street, true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you describe Esad Landzo when you were growing up together in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad was always quiet and withdrawn. As a child, he always had some health problems, so that he couldn't play with us, all those games that we used to play. We mostly played football, soccer. And if he did play with us, he would play only for a short period of time where he would be a goalie because he couldn't run and he couldn't really get physically very active and get tired. He was generally a good guy, a good boy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Court has heard testimony about these health problems, so I won't ask you to go into them other than to just briefly describe in a very short way, the types of problems that he had, why he was not able to play as you've just described.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he had severe problems with breathing. He frequently coughed. And she would get tired quite quickly. I also know that he also had some problems with fingers on the right hand, two or three fingers. I am not sure whether all three or just two fingers. So that he couldn't lift things. And this was due to some kind of wounding, self-wounding with a knife or with a piece of glass, I am not sure really what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now direct your attention back to April of 1992, when the war broke out. You were in JNA military school at the time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When the war broke out, I was in Konjic. I had left the military school in September of '91.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was some six months before. All right. When you left the military school, how far along were you in your training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had left the military school when I was attending at third year of the school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in school in Belgrade, that was the location of the military school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the Court has already heard testimony about the shelling of Konjic and the refugees pouring in and the fear and the panic, so although I am sure you can comment on those, I won't be asking you any questions along those lines, we'll just go directly into what you did during the war, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When the war began, you were a member of the HVO military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of duties did you have as a member of the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a member of the military police of the HVO, I was in charge of securing facilities that were of special importance and also to arrest the military conscripts that did not respond to the call to come to the army. Those were the main tasks that we were executing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point you then became a member of the army military police of Bosnia-Herzegovina army military police; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were your -- how did your duties as a member of that military police differ from the HVO or were they similar, what were your duties as a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, we almost had the same tasks, but here in this military police, we frequently had an opportunity to defend, to go to the defence line of the city, wherever they needed us. This was an additional task that we didn't have in the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll be asking you some questions about that in just a bit. At some point did Esad Landzo become a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that this was about 15 days, so about two weeks after the death of our military policeman in Bradina, which happened on July 12th of '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in the next month in August, there was a swearing in ceremony for the military police; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you attended that ceremony, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Esad Landzo also at that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through another witness, we showed a videotape of that, so I won't be asking you any more questions about the swearing in ceremony at this point, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you were commander of the third platoon of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many platoons were there in the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Esad was under your command as a member of the third platoon, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so were you his direct superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe his demeanour after Celebici, when he became a member of the military police? Demeanour, personality, the way he behaved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (No microphone)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which military police force are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: The only question a few minutes ago, the first question that I asked him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was a member of the HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Correct. And then sort shortly thereafter, he left the HVO military police and became a member --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him. Because at that time, there was no military police of the TO in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: In the beginning, that is correct. So he was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let there be no confusion about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there won't be any confusion, Mr. Gogic, let me back up just a little bit to make the transition from one military police unit to the second military police unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal view?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not necessarily your personal view. The judge asked that I go back and clear something up, just in case there was some misunderstanding about that. So I am just going to back up and ask you a question about when you left the HVO military police and then joined the military police of your army. The judge brought up, and I know that he is correct, that when the war first started, there was not an unit of the military police in the Bosnia-Herzegovina army; isn't that true? And that at some point later, and you tell me, weeks, months, but at some point, then there was established a unit of the military police in the army, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it happened. In the beginning there was just a military police of the HVO, so that means that there was no military police of the TO. And we were practically members of the military police of HVO, beginning of June. So in the beginning of June, military police of the TO was established. And at that time, I transferred into that military police because I deemed that that was the correct thing to do at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And has it been your understanding through my questioning that all of the questions that I have asked you about Esad being a member of the military police, Esad being sworn in in August, et cetera, all the questions along that line, was it your understanding that I was speaking of Esad being a member of the army military police, not the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that clear it up, Your Honour? Did that clear it up? Okay. All right. Let me go back, I believe the last question before we went -- before we backtracked a bit was that I had asked you to describe Esad's behaviour, his demeanour as a member of the military police after he served at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when he came to the military police, Esad was more withdrawn than usual. He was somewhat depressed, perpetually depressed, so that he didn't really socialise with us. For example, when we used to play cards, he would sit by us, somewhere close to us, but he wasn't really always with us. He was simply close by. He was by himself, withdrawn and quiet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're able to make this comparison because you knew him before he went to Celebici and you knew him as a member of your platoon in the military police, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As his platoon commander, you were in charge of giving him orders and assigning him duties; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Esad Landzo respect you and look up to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he follow your rules and did he follow your orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad was a good soldier. And as far as I can remember, he never refused to carry out any of my orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've mentioned -- we've talked a little bit about his breathing difficulties and his hand injury, and you were aware of these, you've testified to that. Did you keep --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- these things in mind, as you assigned him tasks and duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I always had this in mind so that I would always assign him somewhat lighter duties, for example, guarding of the checkpoints, securing -- protecting the hospital and these type of lighter duties where there was no need to be very physically active or carry heavy loads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned guard the hospital, would you give me a specific example of what you mean by guard the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, he was wounded, Mr. Mirsad Catic also known as Cuperak was wounded. And he was at the Konjic Hospital. And, at that time, I assigned Esad to protect him personally at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first began your answer, the English translation that I heard was, he was wounded. Let me just give you a chance to clear that up. You did not say that Esad Landzo was wounded, you're saying that Mr. Mirsad was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirsad Catic was wounded and I assigned Esad to his -- to protect him at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sometimes Esad Landzo's duties took him to the frontlines just the way -- just like other members of the military police; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall a time when you had a mission in Glavaticevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At some point in that mission there were -- you had to climb some hills, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had to climb a hill that was quite steep. And I know that Esad wasn't able to climb up on foot to the top of the hill so that, so that we gave him a horse. And he was riding a horse up to the top of the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point, you had Esad stay behind to watch for deserters, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this happened in the Village of Grusca, where we had left three or four, I don't remember exactly how many military policemen, among one of them was Esad. And I left Esad there exactly due to his health problems so that they were in charge of watching out for the deserters who had left the defence line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long would you say that Esad remained at that post while the rest of you went on farther?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He remained there about 15, 16 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I am going to pass the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURIC
utterances.text: We also have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: The defence counsel of Mr. Hazim Delic has no questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Prosecution, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He feels cheated. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately that puts me back in the hot spot again, though. Your Honours, we had the three witnesses scheduled for today, but Mr. Gogic was the only one who was on the plane yesterday, so we have no further witnesses to present to the Court today and I do apologise. I am not giving up though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You had him and he disclosed the difficulties, at least of one of the witnesses. But there is nothing known about the third one who still hasn't shown up. Have you heard anything from him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that he had spoken to Victim and Witnesses and to our investigator just the night before and assured them that he was in Sarajevo and would meet them at the airport. And he just was a no show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Still hasn't communicated to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where do we go from here?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will be prepared Monday morning to begin with Dr. Gripon. And we'll be prepared to go forward at that point. And, hopefully, we're still going to be on the schedule that we had discussed with the Court last week. So I predict that the Defence of Esad Landzo will be finished at least, at the latest, Wednesday at the close of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that suits the Trial Chamber and we hope that we don't have any more casualties on the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I can assure you we won't have any more missing witnesses on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I have a few motions, which are pending. The top of the list is the Prosecution's notification of witnesses anticipated to testify in rebuttal. And we've also had the Defence, the first defendant's reaction to that motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't have any reaction to our brief on the rebuttal case. We didn't receive anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did file an objection, although I did not receive the filed copy that goes through the Registry, so it appears that it may not have gone through the system, as far as the lawyers are concerned. You may have received it, but I don't believe counsel has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's why we will be able to hear arguments of that motion. I think you're not prepared to argue it now, so we will leave you time when you might have the defence reaction. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, of course, we couldn't add anything else but what we wrote in our brief without reading the defence's reaction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We may defer with the other motion on the procedural aspect, that Hazim Delic's motion for continuance in the alternative, because of the change in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think it's laid out fairly clearly in the motion what our position is, that for reasons known only to the Plenary Session, and I'm not objecting to that or saying it's the wrong procedure, just in the middle of our trial the procedure was changed rather drastically, and we would ask for the relief that we set out, which is either found under rule, I believe, 6C that the defendants would be prejudiced by applying this change in the rules, or in the alternative, after the witnesses are done, let us have a break so we can go out and get punishment witnesses. It's fairly straightforward. It's a request in the alternative, and I personally think that the best procedure would be to apply Rule 6, I believe C, and continue under the prior procedure. But whichever the Trial Chamber thinks is more appropriate is fine with me, just so long as we have some time to prepare punishment evidence for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution takes the side of the defence, as far as this motion is concerned. It is the submission of the Prosecution that for general reasons of rationality, besides the reasons stated by the defence counsel, such an amendment of rules could not apply to a trial like this at the very end of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, what are your real difficulties in adjusting to what the procedure has brought about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we planned our schedules and planned everything based upon both the rules as they existed before July the 10th and the Trial Chamber scheduling order of July 14th. There had been a request for an amendment to that, and so that should come as no surprise to the Trial Chamber. But basically we've scheduled our lives and plans based around that. And if suddenly we're to find that we come back on August 31st and have to be prepared to present evidence relative to punishment, that would be a real problem for us and for the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor may have evidence relevant to punishment they would want to present. I have no feel for that, but there are, of course, a lot of matters in either aggravation or mitigation of punishment which the parties may wish to present to the Trial Chamber, but we thought we would have some period between final arguments when the Trial Chamber took the issue of guilt or innocence under advisement and the delivery of a judgement on those issues to bring in these witnesses, prepare these witnesses, frankly find them. Until now our entire focus, and suspect the entire focus of everybody in the courtroom, has been the issue of guilt and innocence, not the issue of punishment, if there is a conviction on some counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose that would have been the usual thing, and this is where you focus all your attention, so that even if the procedure has changed, and then there was the Trial Chamber to determine punishment, it would not do so without asking you to make a contribution. You never had an idea about what the conviction would be, and nobody starts with a conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and the procedure you're discussing was under the prior rules, and frankly, the procedure that I'm familiar with and I think everyone else is familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Because the prejudice you're suggesting now is such that you should take punishment into account and your address is how could you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you be doing that in your addresses now without knowing exactly what the fate of the accused is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think under the revised rules we would be required to do that, and we're just asking the Trial Chamber to, frankly, for some guidance, and if the Trial Chamber is going to follow the new rules that I set out in the motion, give us some time to get punishment witnesses here. The nightmare, I think, would be for us to argue guilt and innocence and then -- and I'm not saying the Trial Chamber would do this, I just wanted to bring it to the Trial Chamber's attention -- then some weeks later come back and find out we're handed a judgement that says not only guilt and innocence but also has punishment attached to it, which I think is what the new procedure contemplates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually it a laborious one to go ahead and attach punishment, but usually after a conviction then you call on the accused to make any submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree with you completely. It's just my reading of the amended rules that it contemplates that instead of being a bifurcated procedure with a determination of guilt and innocence and then, if necessary, going to punishment, it would be a single procedure. Which again, I dropped a footnote in there saying I'm not complaining about the overall fairness of that, and I know of no reason under the statute why that could not be the procedure. I know of no reason under fundamental fairness why that could not be the procedure. In fact, frankly, in my country our Supreme Court says that constitutionally can be the procedure. So I don't that it's any deprivation of a fair trial. It's just that we need to know how to proceed from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe we're all saying the same thing on this issue, is that we started off believing that we were just putting on evidence of guilt or innocence, and if the Court did perceive right now that the new procedural rules applied, everybody would need to open their case in chief to put on punishment evidence. But since the Court is saying we're going to go by the old rules, you're not going to change them on us in the middle of the game, then we would just proceed under the old rules that we presented evidence of guilt and innocence and once the verdict is rendered you will allow us to put on punishment evidence, as we had assumed from the beginning in this case. Are we all saying the same thing, I think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think we're all saying the same thing. I think we're all agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Nobody has any vested right in any procedure. And so far the procedural amendments can be applied with the one exception: The procedural amendments should not affect any vested rights. To affect the vested right, then the accused has a right he should be tried under the old procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And we have the utmost confidence this Trial Chamber would not let us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Nobody has any vested right in any procedure, except when it takes away a vested right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I feel comfortable with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And when I looked at Rule 6B, which says the procedural rules go into effect immediately, and 6C that says -- excuse me, 6C that says amendment to the rules go into effect immediately but shall not prejudice the rights of the accused. My initial reaction was that the new procedural rules are in effect unless the Trial Chamber finds the application of them would somehow prejudice the defendants. And so what I -- the reason I filed the motion was to say if it's going to -- let's decide what we're going to do in such a way that it does not prejudice my client, and that's why I laid out the two alternatives for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In many jurisdictions where there is no pre-sentencing procedure after conviction, there is something which is called allocutus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we call it right of allocution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In allocutus you allow even evidence to be introduced in mitigation, which is almost equivalent to present it as procedure. So, even if you are now being directed under the new procedure, you will not be deprived of saying something before the sentence is passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It doesn't make any difference whatsoever. The earlier procedure is merely elongating what normally should have been done very briefly by protracting the trial and making all sorts of unnecessary witnesses. You can still do that, but not to the extent to which you invite all sorts of experts to talk about what the conviction should amount to. You are allowed after conviction to call evidence in mitigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And I can think of many things in mitigation that could be presented to the Trial Chamber, everything from mental status to behaviour and the detention facility, all of those things could be mitigating, or for that matter, aggravating, and we just want to make sure we have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you would, yes. You will have every opportunity to lead evidence in mitigation and perhaps the Prosecution, whichever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The other motion which I have is on the competence of one of the judges, and which perhaps, I should mention, should have been brought to notice much earlier than now, because I have dealt with it. I've even also sent it to the Bureau long ago. In fact, they should have dealt with it much earlier than now. And you would have been satisfied about the issue. Why I have gone about it this way, because if you have read it carefully, and I'm sure you have, you will find the rules did not allow for argument before the Trial Chamber. That is why it allowed either the Presiding Judge or the Bureau, and in fact, the Bureau itself does not take such applications, except refer to it by the Presiding Judge. So, if you read rule 15D carefully, you will find it was never intended to be argued, which perhaps was the assumption of counsel. It was not intended to be argued. Because if you rely on such open arguments as the accused has every right under Article 21, everybody accused of any matter has such a right, and we could not be arguing that in the Trial Chamber which is not properly constituted. It would only be two of us, because the person affected will not be. And secondly, the person affected is entitled to representation, because the person's interest is affected. So, in every way you look at it there is no business for arguing it in open court. Now, as I said, the Bureau will definitely rule on the matter. Although, my views have been complicated, because I have the primary duty of making a ruling, and it is only when there is any conflict that it is necessary to refer to them. Here there is no conflict, and I refer to them because of the general position of the trials in this Trial Chamber. Because at every stage things have never looked as if fairness has been involved. So, I think I better refer it to the Bureau, which will take a more impassioned attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Of course, the basic motion never accused anyone of being unfair or having, in the words of rule 15A, personal interest or an association that might affect impartiality. And no one knew on our side that this motion had been referred to the Bureau. If it had been, the motion you have in front of you I don't think ever would have been filed, Your Honour. I think it needs to be made clear that no one is saying that someone, anyone on the Trial Chamber cannot be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have it as a duty, as judges, to assure that everything that is necessary for the impartial administration of this trial has to be assured. We wouldn't be here -- to make sure that all our legal requirements for satisfying a valid trial. We make sure that we have a valid trial. If we find that there are any defects in our procedure, we will not continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I understand that. I'm just standing up kind of as a representative of everybody over here, but I think it needs to be made perfectly clear on the record; there has never been any intent on any part to accuse anyone of any misconduct or unfairness or inability to be fair or anything like that. We view it purely as a legal question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm not even accusing anyone. I'm only explaining the general feeling and the environment of the trial; and therefore, if such a thing affects the Trial Chamber, perhaps let a more prestigious and a more impassioned group look at it, instead of me taking the decision in my own interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, I would never admit there is anyone in this Tribunal more prestigious than this Trial Chamber. You'd never get me to say that. But I understand what you've done, Your Honour, and we appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you will hear from them shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think pending the receipt of the Prosecution, of your motion, I think we might rise. Perhaps, I believe by 12 o'clock you should have that answer. So we come on here for their views. So within one hour I expect that should be solved. The Trial Chamber will now rise and resume at 12

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, have you had an opportunity to read the production of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are ready to argue on the item. With Your Honour's permission, since this is a typically common law issue, Mr. Cowles will argue about that. I will only intervene, if necessary, on any factual issue Mr. Cowles might not be completely aware of. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear you, Mr. Cowles.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: May it please the Court and good afternoon, Your Honours. Addressing the first issue raised by the Defence concerning the proposed calling of the witness, Rajko Dordic. And I do apologise if I mispronounce the names as I am not used to it yet. Concerning that witness, Your Honours, it is the position of the Prosecution is that the calling of this witness in rebuttal is justified as pure rebuttal evidence based on the Defence position. We believe it's pure rebuttal for two reasons, Your Honour. First of all, factually, he will rebut the defence contention, the defence of Mr. Delalic's contention, that this commission, the military investigative commission was in operation. Mr. Dordic will testify that he was released on the third of June, 1992, and his release document does bear that date. It is our position that factually, this rebuts specifically the Defence proposition that the commission could have signed in June as well, but, instead, that Mr. Delalic, we believe it shows specifically that Mr. Delalic signed in June, even though the commission was operating in June. Later in July, I think it is shown that the commission was not operating -- I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who was the chairman of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: That I believe is mentioned as Goran Lokas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Decided on his --

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't understand Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did he sign on his own authority or on the authority on behalf of Goran Lokas?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I believe the document says for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: For whom? The problem is that you've not placed those documents which you want to present now along with your motion, copies of the documents. Have you got a copy of the document with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have it with me. I believe they've been supplied to the Defence. I'll refer to Mr. Turone on that specific issue. I don't have the document with me right now Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why did you not produce the document in the first instance when you were leading your own evidence? Did you examine this witness during the course of your investigations before?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's my information that the office of the Prosecutor was not aware of this witness and did not examine him until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: During the course of the investigations, you did not examine him?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, that is my information that I have been told by the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you have that document, show it to us, a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have now a copy of the English in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, I can forward that to you with the help of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: For Goran Lokas. So you're saying that when the commission was operating, it should have been issued by the commission? Goran Lokas was the chairman of the commission, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your argument that in the presence of the commission, he signed it. How would that help you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You should examine this witness in the first instance and that sign on behalf of Goran Lokas. Who would be the chairman of the commission? How would that help your case further?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we believe that it shows that even though the commission was in operation in June, that Mr. Delalic could sign on behalf of the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: On behalf of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then you have to show evidence that he was a member of the commission. If he was at all in charge, he could have signed it himself instead on behalf of Goran Lokas who was the chairman of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I believe it shows that he was in a position of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How? If he was in a position of authority, he could sign on his own. Why should he sign on behalf of Goran Lokas who was the chairman of the investigative commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'll defer to Mr. Turone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How does this rebut what has been put in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may add something with your permission. The evidence of Jusufbegovic, which we believe Rajko Dordic is supposed to rebut, is the very lines contained in page 11991 of the transcript, when Jusufbegovic said he tried to get in touch in July for the release of the two doctors in July with members of the commission in order to have them sign the release for them, for the two doctors, and he couldn't find any member of the commission at that time and that is the reason why for a very exceptional reason, Zejnil Delalic signed this release form for the commission. The point on which Rajko Dordic should testify is that on 3rd June, when the commission was present every day on a daily basis in Celebici, nevertheless, Delalic signed, although for the commission, without any real need for him to sign for the commission, since the commission was in Celebici on a daily basis in those very days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His evidence that Goran Lokas was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, but the members of the commission were on a daily basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Signed on behalf of Goran Lokas, who was chairman of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have to lead other evidence to show that Goran Lokas himself is not competent to authorise. You will have to have evidence also. You probably have to examine Goran Lokas also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, our argument is that in the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's unnecessary that are not bearing --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, our submission is that at the very beginning of June, when the commission was there on a daily basis in Celebici, and we have all the, a number of release documents, for instance, signed by another member of the commission, other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then you have to explain why should he sign on behalf of Goran Lokas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, that is the evidence you should rebut, that he signed on behalf of Goran Lokas. And if there is any evidence to show that he could not have done that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In the submission of the Prosecution, the fact that Mr. Delalic signed a release document on 3rd June 1992, the fact itself that he signed it on that date, when the members of the commission were on a daily basis present in Celebici, rebuts what Jusufbegovic said, Jusufbegovic and the other witness mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're talking about some other documents, you're talking about release of this particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with this release order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But the evidence given by the Defence witnesses state that the release of the two doctors was done by Delalic in an exceptional situation just because the members of the commission were not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They were authorised by Cerovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Authorised by Goran Lokas. And he said, no, he had an authority to sign on behalf of the investigative commission. In fact, this goes against your case that he was in charge. Why should he be signing on behalf of someone else? When he himself is in charge of Celebici camp, why should he sign on behalf of someone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence evidence given by witnesses Cerovac and Jusufbegovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is in respect of the two doctors. You're talking about the release of this particular gentleman, whom you want to examine as a witness. And signed specifically on behalf of Goran Lokas, who is admittedly the chairman of the commission. Under the rules of procedure of this commission, the chairman is competent to make an order of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see what Your Honour means. But in the submission of the Prosecution, Mr. Delalic on 3rd June did not have any real good reason to sign a release document, since all the members of the commission, except Goran Lokas, but with somebody else acting as president of that commission were present on a daily basis in Celebici. This rebuts the contention of the Defence witnesses, according to whom the two doctors and Miro Golubovic's release should be regarded as very exceptional situations given to the facts that the members were not present in Celebici. This is the argument of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What does it say for the chief of the investigating organ? This means the chief was competent. Maybe the chief spoke to him on the telephone. First, you'll have to examine Goran Lokas also. But he did on his own without consulting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The evidence shows not only Goran Lokas, but the other members of the commission were also competent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Goran Lokas was competent and not in his own to sign the release order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Of course he was. Because after his car accident, he quit the commission and the commission itself could work and function with somebody else acting as president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not a case of rebuttal evidence. It's a case of fresh evidence. Because you did produce two release orders. You did produce a number of these orders signed by Mucic. You did produce release orders signed by Delalic in respect of the two doctors. This is really fresh evidence, not rebuttal evidence. And now you can say that this witness is not available to us, now we've obtained a statement. This is fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It's also fresh evidence because it was not available to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You had two years. The indictment was issued in 1996, why did you not examine all the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the investigation was very, very long and very hard and there are some -- there is some evidence which the Prosecution could obtain only in recent times and the efforts to reach all those documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't call it rebuttal evidence, it's fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see Your Honours' point of view. And in the submission of the Prosecution, there might be some reasons to call it also as rebuttal evidence. But, in any case, even if it is not rebuttal evidence, and this is not our submission, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Make out the case for fresh evidence. You have to make out a case for fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think that we explained enough our point of view as far as the possibility of Rajko Dordic being a rebuttal witness, but I think Mr. Cowles will tell you something else about the other aspect of the situation being anyway all these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Fresh evidence has a different test.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Documents of fresh evidence not previously available to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The test is different. But in all reasonable effort, you could not obtain this evidence earlier. Have you made any effort earlier to contact these detainees?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We've been making efforts all through these last three years in order to get relevant documents for this case. And, unfortunately, some of the relevant documents did not come early enough as to be available for the Prosecution case. And this, I would say, is covered by Rule 67 (d) of the rules of procedure and evidence. But, in any case, these were the factual arguments, which I wanted to add to Mr. Cowles' argument and I will stop here and let Mr. Cowles go ahead. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well, I can't add much more than that, other than we would argue that it's fresh evidence, Your Honours -- I'm sorry. I can't add much more than that. On a second fall-back position, Your Honours, that it would be fresh evidence, newly discovered evidence that is relevant and proper that we could introduce. We did not have this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is the test for allowing fresh evidence after the Defence has almost closed its case? All your efforts which you made, this evidence could not be relevant to you. If you have not made any efforts, then no fresh evidence can be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I understand. And I believe that would be true in your jurisdictions, Your Honours, as well. However, it's my understanding that the Prosecution did not receive this document in its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not a question of receiving, you have a team of authorities and they were in the field, they were examining all the detainees. And with reasonable effort, you could have obtained this evidence. And if you could show that you could not in spite of all that, then, of course, it's a case for fresh evidence. You see, to reopen the whole trial, and the Defence will come up with a list of another twenty witnesses. And then, particularly, this document has been signed on behalf of Goran Lokas, who was admittedly, is the chairman of the investigating commission and the other evidence that he was also injured. And maybe Goran Lokas also told him, please sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am mentioning this to you. And you'll have a long trial going right up to next year. You have to make a case of fresh evidence. And despite all your efforts, you could not get this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: That would be our position, Your Honour, is that this document was among many other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was he one of the detainees at the camp? He was because he got a release order. Why was he not contacted earlier? That's why I ask you, did the OTP examine him during the course of the examination? And you said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I was informed that Mr. Dordic was not examined by the office of OTP during the course of investigation until -- he was not discovered, Your Honour, or found, physically found, until, I believe it's April of this year, 1998, after the closure of the Prosecution case, Your Honour. He physically was not found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have given you the test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually from what you said, you discovered it about the 19th of June this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour the document, I believe, is dated 3 June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: The document arrived here in June of this year, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not a question of arriving here. What efforts are made by the OTP investigator to meet the detainees, particularly this person?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well, I believe, Your Honour, there has been a continuous investigation by our investigators in the field in Bosnia, in Sarajevo, in the attempt over several months to seize relevant documents from different agencies and offices as well as to locate additional witnesses whose names we may have had, but whose physical whereabouts or presence could never be confirmed or located. And that it was only until April of 1998 that Mr. Dordic was finally found and he had the copy of his release document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Now, the Defence is almost finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Apart from that, is this office not available to you before now? The office of the commission, the state commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: That, I don't believe I can comment upon that, I'll defer to Mr. Turone on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you'd done that in April, maybe we would have given more time to the Defence to rebut this document also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the efforts to get in touch and have cooperation from this commission was started early, very early, two years ago, but the cooperation was insufficient for a very long time and until recent times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- was providing you with information about the witnesses. We have heard about an association of detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Of course we had some information from that association, but about the official institutions, the Commission for Prisoners of War, et cetera, we started -- we started very early making our efforts in order to find and receive the relevant documentation, but only in recent time we could reach some better cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When did the OTP first meet Dordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Not one of us ever met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am talking about your investigators in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: They could only get a copy of the document. As I told you, we discovered the existence of this, of this prisoner, this man, sometime in April, I cannot be very precise about dates, I'm sorry, Your Honour. And the release document was obtained by him sometime later and provided to the Prosecution sometime later. And, again, I cannot be quite precise about the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In my jurisdiction, the rules in my jurisdiction are not, of course, applicable here. Whenever you make an application for additional evidence always at the close of trial, you have got to file an affidavit, saying, giving the circumstances. Of course it's not applicable here, but here there has to be some basis on which you say that this evidence, despite best efforts, could not be obtained here. And maybe you have to examine maybe Goran Lokas also, the circumstances under which --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding of a civil law system, things are slightly easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's why I prefaced my statement with that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In the interest of justice demands that the other side should not be taken by surprise in this matter. If there was sufficient reason why you could not have found this document before now, then I would have understood that, why it was. And from what I see, this commission has existed all the time. And your investigation has been on with them. And you could have discovered it with a diligent search. And this is not the time when they could print such evidence, when the purpose is -- without explaining why you could not have done so before now. Let's hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: About this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we have before you, the opposition to this motion, a notification by the Prosecution. I refer Your Honours also to the part of the notification where the Prosecution sets out what this witness' testimony will be. This witness will only produce the document, we are told. He cannot say who signed it or why it is signed for Goran Lokas. We have just heard that they contacted this witness in April, 1998 and disclosure of this document came much later. In other words, they contacted him prior to the close of our Defence case and was disclosed much after we had closed. As Your Honours have pointed out, we say there is no basis for this witness or evidence in rebuttal. And as Your Honours have quite correctly pointed out, the fact that a document is signed for, purportedly signed for someone is all but saying that the document is irrelevant because it does not show who has superior authority over the prisoners at Celebici barracks which Mr. Delalic is accused of being. And we oppose the calling of this witness and this document. This is not proper rebuttal evidence as we have said. And this witness cannot respond directly to what the witnesses, Cerovac and Jusufbegovic testified to in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let's talk about the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The handwriting expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why did you not examine him earlier when there was a dispute about the genuineness of these documents? This issue was raised so many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: It's my understanding, Your Honour, if I may address Your Honour's questions, Professor Stegnar will use the exhibits identified in the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I haven't said that. I said why was it not examined before you closed your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: These are new documents recently seized, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think you want to view the handwriting in respect of the documents which was seized INDA-BAU.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I'm going to have to defer, on a specific document issue I'll defer to Mr. Turone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Aren't these documents which were seized from INDA-BAU on which there was given expert evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let's say that we, as it is explained in our brief, we sort of divide the possible testimony of Mr. -- of Ms. Stegnar into two different parts. There is one part which has to do only with the very new documents which the Prosecution will try to tender through witness Chambers. And, of course, through the one, also, through, with Mr. Rajko Dordic, if he is allowed to testify. But some new documents signed by Zejnil Delalic, which were seized very, very recently, and then the first part of the testimony of Ms. Stegnar is linked to the rebuttal witness Chambers and to the very new documents he could find in these very, very last few weeks. In that part of the testimony Ms. Stegnar is supposed to compare the signatures on these few new documents not previously available to the Prosecution with three authentic signatures of Mr. Zejnil Delalic which are in evidence as part of his OTP statement, or better, as attachment to the OTP statement, exhibit 99-3, and with the signature appearing on Exhibit 127, which was authenticated within the defence case by witnesses Sultanic and Vasogic (Phoen). So this part of the testimony of Ms. Stegnar has really nothing to do with the Vienna exhibits. She is supposed to examine only new documents linked to the testimonial of Mr. Stephen Chambers. The second part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Aren't you then conceding that the other documents obtained from INDA-BAU remain not established that it was written all in the handwriting of Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're only producing the expert with respect to the documents now seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was just saying that this, I've been talking about right now, is the first part of the testimony of Ms. Stegnar on the new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does this mean you are not interested in proving the propensity of the other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We are. I'm coming to the second part now. The first part of the testimony concerns only new documents related to the testimony of Mr. Chambers and Mr. Rajko Dordic. And the witness is supposed to compare those signatures with three authentic signatures in evidence. And the second part of the testimony is linked to the defence witness, what defence witness Kevric said about handwriting and signature on Exhibit 119, which is actually one of the Vienna documents. Exhibit 119 is a short document with seven or ten lines, hand-written, and the signature of Zejnil Delalic. It was shown to the -- to a defence witness, Mr. Kevric who actually recognised the signature of Mr. Delalic. Then in re-examination at question of the defence counsel, he said, "Well, actually, I'm not handwriting expert, it might be a forgery. I do not know." And on this basis and the submission of the Prosecution, this is grounds to rebut this part of re-examination and have the handwriting expert examined also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If he said, "This is not the handwriting of Mr. Delalic," then you could produce evidence. He said "I don't know." So how is it rebuttal now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If he has taken up the position this is not the handwriting of Mr. Delalic, fair enough, you rebut it. But he said I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He said it might be a forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Might be a forgery or might not. It leads to many possibilities. Has he said this is not his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We are all performing our professional duty, of course. We submitted this argument as our argument in order to have Ms. Stegnar testify about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let's analyse it. You see a person make as statement and you want to rebut it by saying it is not true. He is not saying it is not his handwriting. He has not said that. So why the rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't want to be argumentative here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is, I mean, allow me to tell you, this is our legal argument. And this is the argument through which we indicated also a second possible part of the testimony of Ms. Stegnar. But I would like to emphasise that the two parts are different. The first part is not really linked to the Vienna documents. And even if in the last report Ms. Stegnar might have mentioned some other Vienna documents; in any case, the testimony we describe in our brief as for the first part of the testimony concerns only the new documents, and the three handwriting samples we have in evidence, and not the content of the previous report. For the previous report concerning 119 and the other Vienna documents, we felt it was our duty to bring this argument to the Chambers and ask that Ms. Stegnar be allowed to testify also on that. This is what we thought we had to do in our professional duty. This is all I have to say. It may be on legal aspects of all this, Mr. Cowles, who is a common lawyer, might add something if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The principles of civil law and common law are the same. Fair, expeditious trial, nobody to take advantage over the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The very general principles are certainly okay, under the same truth finding process, maybe this is more strong in civil law systems, but as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Might object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But as far as the case in chief and rebuttal case and the specific rules to that, I would say that the civil lawyer would be a little embarrassed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we hear you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We strenuously object to the calling of Professor Stegnar. My learned friend has said that her testimony should only be limited to analysis of newly seized documents based on three known samples. Can I direct Your Honours attention to the notification? The notification has appended to it three expert reports, or two reports and one addendum. The first report dates November 26th, 1997. That's the report that Ms. Stegnar prepared in anticipation of her testimony at that time. And Your Honours will recall that you did not allow the Prosecution to call her. And that was upheld by the Appeals Chamber. She is relying on a report which you said she cannot rely upon in forming her opinions of July 1998, which are the two that I refer to as the other appendices to this notification. And page 7295, that's the hand-written number at the top, I draw your attention to the report of July 17, 1998 wherein Ms. Stegnar refers almost exclusively to the Vienna documents. You will know the Vienna documents are Prosecution documents 104-147. Her report of July is replete with Prosecution exhibits which are the Vienna documents, and the same is true for her addendum of 21 June -- 21 July, pardon me, 1998, wherein she makes reference to the Vienna documents. This amounts to the Prosecution trying to circumvent Your Honours decision and our submission, she should not be allowed to testify in regards to the Vienna documents. This is not an appropriate time to call this witness, when Your Honours ruled in December, and upheld on appeal, we say that the issue is closed. It cannot be revisited. She is not looking at newly seized documents, they are trying to indirectly have her look at the Vienna documents, which is completely contrary to what Your Honours ruled. And there is no way to divide her analysis of newly seized documents with the Vienna documents, as my honourable friend has suggested. In fact, if you look at her report, she co-mingles all the documents in reaching a conclusion. This is an inappropriate form of attempting to use an expert when Your Honours have said the Prosecution cannot, and in our respectful submission she should not be allowed to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I may just add a few words, Your Honours. I feel slightly insulted hearing that I might have tried to circumvent Your Honours. This is not true. I said immediately that Ms. Stegnar's testimony is divided into two parts. And even though she might have considered some other, some Vienna documents in the report of 17 July, I did emphasise earlier that we would not rely on that part of the report of July as far as the first part of the testimony. In the first part of the testimony Ms. Stegnar -- we are not forced to follow the very arguments of any report of an expert witness. In our testimony we would only ask Ms. Stegnar, as far as the first part of her testimony is concerned, we would ask her to examine the signatures appearing as signatures of Zejnil Delalic on some very new documents linked to witness Chambers, and would, we would ask her to compare these signatures with the ones of Exhibit 99-3, and Exhibit 127, just because this was authenticated by Vasogic and Sultanic in the defence case. We would not consider any other part of the last July report of Ms. Stegnar in the first part of the testimony if the first part of the testimony should be admitted alone and the second part should not be admitted. We would, of course, go on to the second part of the testimony on Exhibit 119, et cetera, if Ms. Stegnar is admitted also on this part of the testimony. So, I don't believe I tried to circumvent anybody here. I hope I was clear about this distinction, and if there is any other explanation I should give, please request me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think perhaps let's finish and I deserve to be a little more enlightened as to the basis of the second part of your application, and why you are now relying on this new documents for rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I'm afraid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is part of the testimony of Mr. Chambers, Your Honour, which is not yet objected by the defence of Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have not objected to the gentleman appearing as a witness. You objected to Stegnar appearing, you objected to Dordic appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct, in the written response it's not there, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In your response you objected to Professor Stegnar. You have not objected to Chambers appearing as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct. That's not in the written report, or the written objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you have no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We say that Prosecution has the burden of proving it's rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you have not objected to it in the motion moved by the Prosecution. Four witnesses have been mentioned, one is Dordic and the other is Dr. Stegnar, and as far as you're concerned where is Chambers? You have said Stegnar should not appear and you said Dordic should not appear, but you have not said a word about Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That was not part of our objection in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You don't object to Chambers appearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We say the Prosecution must show when he's here that this is rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are talking about fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We say the whole time the Prosecution must satisfy Your Honours that it is rebuttal and not fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Now they want to produce fresh evidence. You have not said a word about it in your motion, response to the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You should have said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Specifically. But that perhaps has provoked me to ask Mr. Turone what actually is the basis of the objection? Because they have now asked for Mr. Chambers to come up to give some evidence, which as far as I'm aware has nothing to do with the rebuttal. It is entirely new. My view is that perhaps even if you did not advert to it, the Trial Chamber has a duty to point out areas which perhaps might have alluded counsel. But if Mr. Turone would be more helpful, you can give us the background of why you want that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not as for rebuttal. Except you want to assume that it is rebuttal evidence, but I did not understand it to be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But again, Your Honours, if you allow me, since I -- in my system rebuttal evidence and fresh evidence are treated in a different way than in common law. But I believe that what I could say on the matter of general principles of law, and again I will ask Mr. Cowles to add something, the documents, or some of the documents Mr. Chambers will produce have also a rebutting effectiveness. And I would say that this might be better determined and evaluated by the Chambers, by Your Honours, when Mr. Chambers will be here and will testify about his investigation and the reasons why this investigation could give some results only in July. On the other hand, documents arrived only in July, in the very last days, I would say, certainly fresh evidence, which in the -- well, I'm missing the word now, I'm sorry. Your Honours might evaluate and determine whether to accept him on the basis of Rule 67, paragraph b. And the fact that -- I suppose, the fact that the Defence counsel did not include objections in their motion is that they expect to see what happens when Mr. Chambers takes the stand. And I expect them to be very aggressive, maybe, but to do that at that time. And this is why I would ask Your Honours to wait for Mr. Chambers to be on the stand in order to evaluate, then, the fresh evidence and rebuttal evidence which he might produce. I don't know if this is sufficient. If it is not, I again would ask Mr. Cowles to add anything he might be willing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you for presenting that properly. If you're not presenting evidence in rebuttal but as evidence discovered thereafter, and which you've properly informed the other party, then perhaps it is part of the provision of Rule 67D. Whether it is proper to be admitted for the purposes is a different matter, and we will determine in the course of the proceedings as a whole. But you regard it as evidence which you have now discovered which you think is reasonable to be included as part of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could have a final word. Two points: First, we say it is the burden on the Prosecution to show the Chamber that it's rebuttal evidence and not fresh evidence. And the second point is this: I come back to Professor Stegnar and ask Your Honours to look at her report of 17 July and the addendum of 21 July, and with all due respect to my learned colleague, you cannot separate, as Mr. Turone has suggested, her views on the Vienna documents, which Your Honours said she cannot testify to, and her views on new documents. Her report is based almost entirely on a comparison with Vienna documents. She can't come here and testify and say I'm going to blank that out of my mind for the purposes of my testimony. She has prepared a report last November, she prepared the one in July based on that report in large part and makes specific reference to documents Your Honours say she cannot rely upon. So it's incorrect, in my submission, to say that somehow she can play mental gymnastics and ignore her conclusions which are right here, which form the basis of her opinion. And for that reason we say she should not testify. I will sit down after making one other observation.
