If Officer Chambers is allowed to testify, the issue there is one of search and seizure and chain of custody, I would ask that on the issue of admissibility be deferred to sometime after direct examination, cross-examination and submissions, if any, on issues of admissibility on the chain of custody, if Your Honours rule that Mr. Chambers can testify, as a procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The question of admissibility cannot be determined until we see the documents themselves and determine what they are. The application before us is for permission to introduce these documents. And if your opposition is that it is improper to do so because of the arguments which you have raised, then so be it. But that is not the issue. The argument of the Prosecution is that these are new documents which have just been found and which were not found before now, and they would like to introduce them. Now, that is quite different from Chambers. The Chambers argument is different from that of Professor Stegnar. Professor Stegnar is trying to authenticate the handwriting of your client in order to corroborate whatever has been before the Trial Chamber. This is what that evidence is seeking to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We say the evidence presented at this time must be limited to rebuttal, and as far as Professor Stegnar goes, she is not a competent expert because of your ruling of last December and a reading of her report of a few weeks ago, which relies almost entirely on her analysis carried out at the time of November, December 1997. She can't separate in her own mind to testify between these two reviews of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask to add just a few words? It's not a matter of separating something in the head of an expert witness. I said that in my opinion whatever be the report submitted by the expert witness, the examining part might decide not to rely on part of that report and limit the testimony on some specific points. And for the first part of the testimony of Ms. Stegnar, as I said, is a matter of comparing the signatures of the fresh evidence of the new documents with the three samples already in evidence. And that's nothing to do with Vienna documents. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: About Mr. Chambers, he has discovered these documents now, after a search of the records of the Konjic Municipal Headquarters, the TO, whatever it is, the Bosnian army; why was this search not carried out earlier? You see the basic theme of all these trials, whether they take the civil laws or the common laws, is an expeditious and fair trial. Expeditiousness is as important and is really relevant in the context of a fair trial. Why was this search not carried out earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Chambers is in a position to explain exactly what were all the efforts done by the investigating team, and he will be in a position to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before he comes himself, you must give us a statement on that. Why was it not this search carried out earlier? He is your witness and you have to satisfy us that this could not have been done earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We might ask Mr. Chambers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you must ask him first, you're the Prosecutor, and satisfy us before we allow Mr. Chambers to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We will ask Mr. Chambers to prepare a statement explaining all this and file that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Statement to the extent why the search was not carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, nobody is accusing you for not finding a thing which ought to have been found and handed to you for the purposes of your case. The substantive argument in all questions of this nature is that with reasonable diligence this document could have been found before now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not that it has not been found, could have been found. The institution has been there. His offices were there. And if they had actually done it in the proper way, they could have been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see Your Honour's point and I agree with that as a matter of principle. And I would say that Mr. Chambers is in a position to explain that all was done with due diligence and there is an explanation why all this came out and had the result only these last few weeks. But if I have not misunderstood Your Honours' request, Your Honours want Mr. Chambers to let Your Honours have the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not Mr. Chambers, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I mean the Prosecution have a statement of Mr. Chambers explaining all this. Is this what I have been requested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The statements of Mr. Chambers may be the basis of the Prosecution's case. You have to tell us. The statement of what Mr. Chambers' said may be the basis of your explaining why this was not done earlier. We're not interested in the statement of Mr. Chambers, we're interested in the statement of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. All right, Your Honour, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You see the first thing that provokes my inquiry was when in your motion you indicated that he will testify on the 19th June 1998, he carried out searches of the premises, including Canada. Now, this is so many months away from one intensive investigation about this matter was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour is right. It happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It becomes unpardonable to imagine that you can now come and tell us that you have not found such relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This happened after an enormous number of requests, letters to the representative of the Bosnian government at the embassy here in The Hague. A large number of efforts which would be explained to Your Honours with this statement and further explanation by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You've got so many documents of a like nature from the same commission, state commission, for the missing. We've got so many records from them and we've been dealing with them. Because the burden is on you to show that you could not have found this document at the time when you made the investigation. It is only on that basis that the Trial Chamber will be able to give you the relief. Because it's not enough to wait for him to come and tell us why he could not have, he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: His Honour Karibi-Whtye has said what I was thinking and that is that we're in the second year of this trial, and, perhaps, the third or fourth year of investigations concerning these matters. And the Prosecution, despite what they say, despite what reasons they may offer, I think is a matter of law. It's unfair at this point to produce documents in June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is also a psycho, forensic expert you want to examine. Maybe you've got a case on that, even to introduce a new defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was not a free agent. He had independent personality and he was doing everything to please his superiors. Your defence is basically this is a new element and I think the Prosecution has a right to rebut that, to express in this regard and not realise it. Even if they're reliable, they do not lead to a plea of diminished liability.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're not objecting because under any common law system, or any system that I am aware of, this is proper rebuttal evidence and I had expressed my lack of objections to the Prosecution earlier, so I believe that is totally proper. If I had an objection that I could stand by, I certainly would have offered it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we'll grant the first relief definitely. Your application to call an expert witness, Dr. Landy Sparr, we grant that. But I am not satisfied that Rajko Dordic would be a suitable witness for rebuttal. You have not given enough sufficient background why Stephen Chambers would come to give new evidence, which is -- actually, I really didn't see the value of Professor Stegnar, except you want Professor Stegnar to come and give evidence on the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may address the issue of Investigator Chambers, I agree certainly with Your Honours' permission that we should present to the Court facts showing why this evidence is fresh; why it could not have been seized earlier by the exercise of reasonable diligence during the course of a very lengthy investigation. I agree with Your Honours and that is completely appropriate. I would ask the Court leave to, perhaps, amend, to file as soon as possible by the first part of next week, an addendum to our proposal concerning Mr. Chambers and the efforts of the investigation to seize documents and why these documents are new, fresh documents have just now been seized factually. If we could provide to the Chamber those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am sure you come from common law. You can't keep the trial hanging on.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I agree with that. I understand, Your Honours. I would just ask the Court's indulgence to be allowed to supplement that factually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Anyway, I think she's concluding her evidence next week. You said Wednesday as the last day. You can bring your expert, this forensic, science expert Thursday or Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and he will be available to testify Tuesday or Wednesday, if we're able to conclude Ms. McMurrey's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Make it Thursday or Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thursday or Friday. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thursday morning on the condition --

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: I believe we've been planning all along to be able to present him mid-week, so that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please do that, so that we don't waste any more time, otherwise, we'll have three free days off.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: We're ready to proceed. As I said with Dr. Sparr, we will be ready Wednesday, if we can present him. In fact, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does that suit you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I feel so confident that they'll be completed with Dr. Sparr by the end of Friday, that I have made my reservations to leave at 7.30 Friday evening. And my niece is getting married Saturday, August, 1st. So I feel very confident that that part will be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Have I understood your ruling that witnesses Dordic, Chambers and Stegnar will not be called?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think Dordic, his evidence is not rebuttal evidence and Chambers hasn't given enough grounds for calling in new evidence. And, similarly, Stegnar, there is no basis for Stegnar. The only evidence which definitely falls within the rebuttal rule is Dr. Sparr.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I have just a moment to confer with Mr. Turone? Thank you, Your Honours, we have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's all we have for today. Well, we spent the week with comparative leisure. I did not expect that. I hope we'll do better next week and not waste so much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And allow Ms. McMurrey to attend the wedding of her niece.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: If I may just clarify. If Ms. McMurrey's case is finished by, say, Tuesday evening, is it the Court's intention that we can proceed into Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Any time she finishes, if you can call your next witness, offer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did I understand that Ms. McMurrey has only witness Gripon and nobody else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, we don't know more than Gripon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There might be other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's the Defence. I wouldn't know what the Defence has in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am still hoping for the one who got sick at the airport to make a miraculous recovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So we'll see you on Monday at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
